extracted.intended_audience: Stanford inventors (faculty, staff, students) and other university researchers interacting with the Office of Technology Licensing
extracted.subtask_description: Step-by-step institutional process and expectations from confidential invention disclosure through evaluation, patenting, marketing, negotiation, licensing, monitoring, income distribution, and amendments; emphasizes inventor responsibilities and how OTL makes commercialization decisions. Specific to Stanford OTL's practices and policies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure (Invention and Technology Disclosure Form)
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventors must confidentially disclose new ideas by submitting an Invention and Technology Disclosure Form to OTL. The submission creates a record of the invention (descriptive information), the inventor(s) involved, who sponsored the work, and public disclosures and publications. For inventions from a PI's laboratory, the PI's authorization is required even if the PI is not an inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a description of the technology and explain the critical solution it could provide to benefit society. The disclosure serves as the starting point for OTL's docketing and evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manager Assignment (docketing and licensing manager responsibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclosures received by OTL are logged, assigned a docket number, and assigned to a specific licensing manager. This manager is responsible for all actions relating to the docket going forward.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect a single licensing manager to be your point of contact and to coordinate subsequent evaluation, prosecution, marketing, negotiations, and post-license monitoring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation (feasibility, patentability, novelty, market potential)
rubrics_metrics.description: The licensing manager and inventor(s) discuss the invention and make a preliminary evaluation of manufacturing feasibility, patentability, novelty, potential applications, and possible markets. OTL may decide not to pursue commercialization if patenting is unlikely or licensing prospects are poor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factors that can reduce the chance of pursuing protection include prior publication, insufficient data, small potential market, or high development costs. Inventors may assist with prior art searches and are invited to suggest licensing strategies (e.g. exclusive vs. non-exclusive). Guidance/examples: basic scientific tools likely licensed non-exclusively; inventions requiring significant company investment typically licensed exclusively to give licensees incentive to invest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent Application (when to file and inventor role)
rubrics_metrics.description: OTL does not file patent applications for all disclosures. The licensing manager must weigh the chance of successful patenting and licensing against the cost of obtaining patent protection (approximately $30,000–$45,000 in the U.S.). If pursuit is warranted, OTL will work with inventors and a patent attorney or agent to prepare the application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Considerations against filing: prior publication, insufficient supporting data, or poor licensing prospects. The inventor's expertise is crucial during drafting and prosecution because the attorney may lack the detailed technical insight that demonstrates novelty and non-obviousness. Inventors will be asked about contributions to determine correct inventorship; see Inventorship FAQ for more detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marketing (preparing non-confidential abstracts and outreach)
rubrics_metrics.description: OTL markets technologies to prospective companies as part of developing a licensing strategy. Marketing involves preparing a non-confidential abstract that is posted on OTL's website and sent to targeted companies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inventor input is appreciated on technical and market feasibility and on leads for potential licensees; inventors often provide the best leads. If a company requests additional technical information, OTL usually asks inventors to provide it and can use confidentiality agreements when necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negotiations (license proposals, flexibility, and inventor involvement)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a company expresses strong interest, the licensing manager begins negotiations, starting with a license proposal and proceeding through negotiations that may require flexibility and creativity to reach a mutually satisfactory agreement. Terms vary depending on technology, market, and company.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: startups may offer equity or deferred payments instead of large upfront fees. The inventor's role during negotiations is generally limited but may include evaluating a company's capacity to develop licensed products. If an inventor has a potential conflict of interest (COI), they must participate in a COI review. Note: only about 20–25% of disclosures are ultimately licensed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitoring Progress (post-license oversight)
rubrics_metrics.description: After a license is signed, the licensing manager monitors the licensee's performance for the duration of the license, typically via periodic financial or development reports required under most agreements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both license terms and company progress reports are generally treated as confidential business information. Monitoring ensures compliance with development milestones and payment obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent Income Sharing (royalty & equity distribution rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: After deductions for OTL operations and reimbursement of direct expenses (e.g., patent and legal costs not paid by licensees), distributable Patent Income from a single license is divided according to Stanford policy. For the first $3,000,000 of cumulative distributable income: 33.34% to the inventor, 24.66% to the inventor's department, 21.0% to the inventor's school, and 21.0% to the office of the VPDOR. For cumulative income exceeding $3,000,000: 33.34% to the inventor, 14.66% to the inventor's department, 26.0% to the inventor's school, and 26.0% to the office of the VPDOR.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Department and school royalties must be used for research or educational purposes only. In multiple-inventor cases, OTL will divide the inventors’ share equally unless all inventors agree otherwise. For portfolios licensed under a single license, OTL allocates earned royalties only to the docket(s) covering the specific revenue-generating products or services; revenue is attributed to dockets based on patent/technology coverage. Inventors on dockets that do not cover the licensed products will not receive earned royalties from that license (though they may receive other income types such as maintenance fees).

rubrics_metrics.name: Amending Licenses (modifying agreements over time)
rubrics_metrics.description: Either party can request an amendment to a license agreement at any time during its life to adapt to changed circumstances as technologies, companies, and markets evolve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Amendments are negotiated by the licensing manager. Expect renegotiation when business models, development plans, or market conditions change.
